title: 5G Sensing for Human Pose Estimation with PRS-based CSI: An Experimental Demonstration
summary: This paper presents an experimental study of device- free 2D human pose estimation using Channel State Information (CSI) extracted from downlink Fifth Generation (5G) Positioning Reference Signal (PRS). The proposed system employs a Next Generation Node Base (gNB) transmitting PRS to a User Equipment (UE) equipped with two receive antennas to measure the radio channel. The CSI is estimated using a least-squares (LS) method, and processed through amplitude smoothing and phase calibration. The resulting amplitude and phase representations are used as inputs to a deep learning model for pose estimation. We compare amplitude-only input with joint amplitude-phase training at a bandwidth of 20 MHz. The joint training outperforms the amplitude-only solution and achieves Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK) equal to 32.2%, 72.9%, and 84.2% below 10%, 30%, and 50% of the distance between left shoulder and right hip, respectively. These results demonstrate that standardized downlink 5G PRS-based CSI contains useful information for human pose estimation, even with a simple radio configuration and a relatively small dataset.

title: Coordinated and Uncoordinated Channel Tracking for High-Rate IoT in Distributed Massive MIMO With Low-Resolution ADCs
summary: This paper investigates dynamic channel tracking for high-rate Internet of things (IoT) in distributed massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) with low-resolution analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), where pilot and data activities are decoupled, pilots are reused, and mobile channels evolve across access slots. We hereby develop a quantization-aware joint coordinated Kalman filter (Q-JCKF) for known pilot activity and a quantization-aware distributed probabilistic data association filter (Q-DPDAF) for uncoordinated access. For uplink analysis, we derive a closed-form statistical use-and-then-forget (UatF) expression for Q-JCKF and mixture-aware, pilot-conditioned, and long-term statistical UatF formulations for Q-DPDAF, together with the large-N pilot-reuse ceiling and a cross-access point (AP) association term with an O(epsilon) posterior-concentration bound. The proposed framework recovers JC-KF/PDAF in the ideal-ADC co-located limit, and quantifies the conditional loss of Kalman measurement information caused by finite-resolution quantization. We further characterize computational, memory, and fronthaul scaling: Kronecker-structured Q-JCKF reduces covariance-processing complexity, while groupwise Q-DPDAF limits hypothesis enumeration from 2^K to 2^{K_r} and enables parallel AP-local processing. Simulations corroborate the analytical and complexity outcomes, quantify ADC-resolution and pilot-access effects, and demonstrate improved lower-tail spectral efficiency, robust mobility tracking, near-ideal 4-bit performance, reliable Q-DPDAF activity inference, and substantial runtime reductions over legacy implementations and processing frameworks.

title: A Theory of Transmit-Receive-Manifold of Single-Photon Quantum-Dot Antenna Arrays
summary: A quantum-dot array that receives a single photon is a collectively coupled antenna, and its receive manifold is not always the plane-wave manifold. So, this work aims to develop a complete transmit-channel-receive manifold model for quantum dot (QD) arrays. For the sake of validation, it considers a reference target pattern which can be obtained using classical array excitation.

title: Adaptive Calibration of RF Digital Twins via Budget-Constrained Radio Measurement Selection
summary: Radio-frequency (RF) digital twins (DTs) enable site-specific wireless propagation prediction by explicitly reconstructing the physical environment and modeling electromagnetic interactions. Although physics-based DTs reduce reliance on exhaustive measurements, systematic bias relative to real radio data arises from environmental uncertainty, material inaccuracies, and geometric abstractions. Calibration using field measurements is therefore necessary but costly under limited sampling budgets. This paper studies active RF DT calibration, in which measurement locations are selected sequentially and in an online manner to estimate a calibration offset under strict measurement budget constraints. A physics-based RF DT pipeline is developed, integrating semantic geospatial data from OpenStreetMap, 3D modeling in Blender, and deterministic ray tracing in Sionna to capture dominant building and foliage effects. This RF DT is calibrated using path-loss measurements collected with software-defined radios. Multiple online calibration strategies that select radio measurement locations are compared, including random sampling, rank-structured sampling with balanced coverage, quasi-Monte Carlo ranked selection, progressive structure-aware allocation, and fully adaptive uncertainty-driven sampling with estimator stabilization. Results demonstrate that adaptive and structure-aware schemes significantly improve both mean and worst-case calibration accuracy, particularly in the low-budget regime for radio measurements.

title: Sensitivity of RMS Delay Spread Estimation to Power Delay Profile Thresholding in Time-Varying Channels at 33 GHz
comment: 5 pages, 7 figures
summary: Root mean square (RMS) delay spread is a key parameter characterizing temporal dispersion in radio propagation channels. Its estimation from measured power delay profiles (PDPs), however, depends strongly on the adopted power threshold. This paper investigates the sensitivity of RMS delay spread estimates to relative PDP thresholding in a time-varying millimeter-wave channel at 33 GHz. The analysis uses wideband channel sounding measurements conducted in a dynamic road environment with moving vehicles. The temporal evolution and empirical cumulative distributions of RMS delay spread are evaluated for thresholds ranging from -20 to -50 dB. Reducing the threshold increases the median RMS delay spread from approximately 140 to 168 ns and the 90th percentile from 200 to 210 ns. Both statistics converge at lower thresholds, with -40 dB providing a practical convergence level. The results emphasize the importance of threshold selection for reliable channel characterization and consistent comparison of measurements.

title: Digital Twin-Guided Wireless Localization via Probabilistic Inverse Learning
summary: This work investigates how site-specific digital twins (DTs) can support wireless localization using simplified distributed infrastructure. We propose PRISM (Probabilistic Refinement using Inverse learning and a Site-specific Model), a DT-guided probabilistic localization scheme with single-antenna access points (APs). Localization is formulated as a probabilistic inverse problem in which a conditional proposal distribution over UE locations is learned from multi-node channel impulse responses (CIRs). The proposal generates candidate locations, with its spread regularized during training and DT consistency used to reweight candidates and refine the estimate at inference. The DT serves as an approximate forward-consistency model, avoiding assumptions of exact channel fidelity or differentiability with respect to user position. Numerical experiments demonstrate gains over data-driven and classical fingerprinting benchmarks, while achieving a median error of approximately $0.7$ m using 10 single-antenna APs. Without retraining, PRISM remains effective under degraded inference-time DT features. PRISM also yields uncertainty estimates from its proposal covariance, with empirical $χ^2$ calibration approaching ideal behavior as APs increase.

title: Deep Holes and Aperture: Sign Laws for the Empirical Correlation of Lattice-Sampled Random Wave Fields
comment: 22 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory
summary: A Gaussian random wave field is sampled on a lattice within a bounded aperture. After displacement, re-indexing leaves a residual in the Voronoi cell. We study whether the empirical lag correlation has positive real part throughout the cell. For each realization in a single-output reciprocal link with noiseless over-the-air return, this is equivalent to the negative returned gradient being a descent direction for all residuals and differentiable losses with nonzero error signals. Return noise is treated exactly. For isotropic fields, ball-shaped apertures, unshifted lattice points, and dilations approaching the critical covering radius, every minimizer is a deep hole except with exponentially small probability. A Gaussian vector on the deep holes determines the limiting failure probability, with explicit covariance and lattice-independent limiting normalization. Square, hexagonal, simple cubic, and body-centered cubic lattices have two, three, four, and twelve sign classes. At fixed target failure probabilities below the critical limiting value, this covariance determines the exact leading aperture constant. When the margin and target failure probability vanish jointly, that constant is common to lattice shapes within each dimension. A cubic correction yields vanishing relative tail error in a moderate-deviation regime. A non-asymptotic two-sided aperture law has explicit constants. With a Rayleigh-faded specular path and positive diffuse margin, a failure floor occurs at every positive path power exactly when the cosine of its phase change is negative somewhere in the cell. The floor vanishes for all directions exactly when the covering radius is at most a quarter wavelength.
